Google released [Gemma 4](https://huggingface.co/blog/gemma4) this week. Reviewing the architecture, I noticed a familiar mechanism — Per-Layer Embeddings (PLE), first shipped in [Gemma 3n](https://ai.google.dev/gemma/docs/gemma-3n) last year and never formally published. It looked familiar because DeepSeek's [Engram](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.07372), submitted six months later, does the same thing.

Engram was billed as "a new axis of sparsity" and "a missing primitive." But the core operation — retrieve a learned embedding from an off-GPU table, gate it against the hidden state, modulate, inject into the residual stream — was already in production. Google just never wrote the paper!

## The mechanism, side by side

Much of the community's understanding of PLE comes from [antimatter15's reverse-engineering work](https://github.com/antimatter15/reverse-engineering-gemma-3n).

PLE maintains a learned embedding table per transformer layer. At each layer:

1. **Retrieve** a learned vector by token ID.
2. **Gate** via a projection of the hidden state through a non-linearity.
3. **Modulate** by element-wise multiplication.
4. **Inject** back into the residual stream.

Engram performs the same four operations. The difference is the retrieval key: where PLE indexes by single token ID, Engram indexes by hashed N-gram sequence. Set N=1 and the hash reduces to a direct lookup. PLE is the unigram case of Engram.

The remaining differences — which layers carry tables, naming conventions, exact dimensionality — are implementation choices, not architectural ones.

## What Engram genuinely adds

The N-gram generalisation is non-trivial: it requires hashing, collision handling, and vocabulary compression. The sparsity allocation law (20–25% of sparse parameters to memory, the rest to MoE) is a useful empirical finding. The DRAM offloading analysis — a 100B-parameter table served from host memory at under 3% throughput penalty — is practically important. The mechanistic analysis showing the module frees early layers from static pattern reconstruction is illuminating.

Engram cites classical N-gram models, word2vec, Bojanowski, Borgeaud, and DeepSeek's own MoE work. It does not cite or mention PLE.

DeepSeek are doing great work and publishing it. Their architecture contributions are genuinely frontier-advancing.

But lineage matters, and it looks like this one starts with Google's PLE.
